evidence.title: Advances in Computer Vision and Sensor-Based Methods for Intelligent Power Transmission Line Inspection.
evidence.abstract: Electricity is fundamental for all modern infrastructures, while disruptions in transmission networks could result in severe failures in healthcare, transportation, communication, industry, and all related to public safety. However, inspection of overhead lines and their components is costly and labor-intensive. The convergence of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), advanced imaging sensors, and deep-learning-based Computer Vision has reshaped this domain. To this end, this work presents a systematic review of Computer Vision applications in electric power transmission line inspection. From an initial 1493 Scopus records, 148 studies published between 2018 and 2026 were retained through a transparent, multi-stage screening and quality-scoring process based on PRISMA guidelines. The reviewed literature was synthesized across four axes: (1) monitoring platforms and sensor technologies, (2) Computer Vision approaches per vision task, (3) datasets, metrics, and evaluation practices, and (4) synthesis of results and industrial adoption. The analysis of the literature confirms the dominance of You Only Look Once (YOLO) family models for real-time edge deployment and the rising adoption of Transformer architectures, while exposing persistent gaps in dataset availability, domain generalization, and field validation. The review concludes with the open challenges and concrete future directions toward fully autonomous, robust, and sustainable inspection systems.

evidence.title: A systemic vulnerability in child protection: the interprofessional gap in abuse and neglect recognition rooted in university curricula.
evidence.abstract: Background/objectives The integrity of child protection systems, a precondition for social sustainability, is compromised by an 'interprofessional awareness gap' among key sentinel professions, particularly within health and education. This study aims to empirically define this gap by comparing the preparedness of two critical future professional cohorts: final-year midwifery and pre-school education students. The objective is to reveal how their distinct university curricula shape foundational awareness of child abuse and neglect (CAN) before they enter professional practice. Methods Using a causal-comparative design, this study assessed final-year midwifery ( n = 246) and pre-school education ( n = 115) undergraduates in Türkiye. Two validated psychometric instruments measured awareness across distinct subtypes of abuse and neglect, revealing the multifaceted nature of their understanding. Results Findings revealed a significant disparity, with future midwives being less prepared to identify CAN than their education counterparts. This awareness deficit was most pronounced for subtle forms of maltreatment, such as emotional and economic abuse, and all dimensions of neglect. A student's academic department was the sole significant predictor of awareness, outweighing the influence of academic progression or prior training. Conclusion This gap represents a systemic vulnerability cultivated by siloed higher education paradigms. Midwifery's traditional biomedical curriculum appears insufficient for imparting the holistic, socio-ecological perspective required for effective safeguarding. A paradigm shift toward mandatory Interprofessional Education (IPE) is imperative. Such reform is crucial for forging a shared professional ethos and a common language of risk, thereby creating a truly resilient and sustainable child protection framework.

evidence.title: A lightweight insulator defect detection algorithm based on drone images for power line inspection
evidence.abstract: Accompanying the enhancement of unattended systems based on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and UAV base station, the lightweight model deployment of unattended systems is of great significance for inspecting the condition of transmission power lines and ensuring the safe and stable operation of the power grid. Current insulator defect detection methods are tasked with small–object detection in complex environments, with their accuracy often improved by optimizing network structures only. Considering both parameter and computational efficiency, we developed LFL–YOLO (LSDHead–FINs–LAMP–YOLOv8n) that is suitable for edge computing. Before the spatial pyramid transmits feature maps to the detection head, some levels are skipped based on inter–level sparsity, and the model’s ability to perceive scale and task-aware attention for complex backgrounds and small objects is dynamically enhanced. By combining this with spatial attention, a high–performance LSDHead is proposed. Secondly, a lightweight FINs is proposed to improve the neck of YOLOv8. This structure ensures effective interaction and feature penetration across different channels of local features. Finally, layer–adaptive unstructured pruning based on magnitude is performed. The pruned model not only reduces computational complexity and model size, significantly improving the model’s real–time performance, but also enhances detection accuracy. Lastly, to align more closely with real–world engineering applications, this study uses public datasets to verify the model’s generalization effect and validates the practical application effect on a dataset. Experimental results show that compared to the current benchmark, LFL–YOLO achieves significant improvements in accuracy and inference speed. Specifically, LFL–YOLO achieves an accuracy of 97.4%, compared to YOLOv8n, reduces the number of parameters by 23.5% and decreases computation by 9.6%. The proposed method has practical applicability in obtaining aerial images of transmission lines in complex environments.

Current insulator defect detection methods are tasked with small–object detection in complex environments, with their accuracy often improved by optimizing network structures only. Considering both parameter and computational efficiency, we developed LFL–YOLO (LSDHead–FINs–LAMP–YOLOv8n) that is suitable for edge computing. Before the spatial pyramid transmits feature maps to the detection head, some levels are skipped based on inter–level sparsity, and the model’s ability to perceive scale and task-aware attention for complex backgrounds and small objects is dynamically enhanced. By combining this with spatial attention, a high–performance LSDHead is proposed. Secondly, a lightweight FINs is proposed to improve the neck of YOLOv8. This structure ensures effective interaction and feature penetration across different channels of local features. Finally, layer–adaptive unstructured pruning based on magnitude is performed. The pruned model not only reduces computational complexity and model size, significantly improving the model’s real–time performance, but also enhances detection accuracy. Lastly, to align more closely with real–world engineering applications, this study uses public datasets to verify the model’s generalization effect and validates the practical application effect on a dataset. Experimental results show that compared to the current benchmark, LFL–YOLO achieves significant improvements in accuracy and inference speed. Specifically, LFL–YOLO achieves an accuracy of 97.4%, compared to YOLOv8n, reduces the number of parameters by 23.5% and decreases computation by 9.6%. The proposed method has practical applicability in obtaining aerial images of transmission lines in complex environments.

warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-016 (sharpened per CEO Round 58): A proposed latent quantity survives only when (1) identifiability is demonstrated under an EXPLICIT observation/dynamics model with full rank/observability analysis (not naive unknown-count), AND (2) identifiability REMAINS under plausible model uncertainty (each ideal assumption relaxed toward realistic physics and re-tested). A single favorable rank calculation under a convenient model is INSUFFICIENT. A single unfavorable perturbation model is ALSO INSUFFICIENT to claim universal non-identifiability — it only kills the specific estimator tested under that specific perturbation model. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.

When in doubt, the implementation is killed; the scientific question stays open until either (a) a survivor is found or (b) an explicit non-identifiability counterexample is constructed (two physically distinct latent states producing indistinguishable observations under ALL measurement protocols).

warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Electricity is fundamental for all modern infrastructures, while disruptions in transmission networks could result in severe failures in healthcare, transportation, communication, industry, and all related to public safety. However, inspection of overhead lines and their components is costly and labor-intensive. The convergence of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), advanced imaging sensors, and deep-learning-based Computer Vision has reshaped this domain. To this end, this work presents a systematic review of Computer Vision applications in electric power transmission line inspection. From an initial 1493 Scopus records, 148 studies published between 2018 and 2026 were retained through a transparent, multi-stage screening and quality-scoring process based on PRISMA guidelines. The reviewed literature was synthesized across four axes: (1) monitoring platforms and sensor technologies, (2) Computer Vision approaches per vision task, (3) datasets, metrics, and evaluation practices, and (4) synthesis of results and industrial adoption. The analysis of the literature confirms the dominance of You Only Look Once (YOLO) family models for real-time edge deployment and the rising adoption of Transformer architectures, while exposing persistent gaps in dataset availability, domain generalization, and field validation. The review concludes with the open challenges and concrete future directions toward fully autonomous, robust, and sustainable inspection systems.

custody_records.raw_content: Background/objectives The integrity of child protection systems, a precondition for social sustainability, is compromised by an 'interprofessional awareness gap' among key sentinel professions, particularly within health and education. This study aims to empirically define this gap by comparing the preparedness of two critical future professional cohorts: final-year midwifery and pre-school education students. The objective is to reveal how their distinct university curricula shape foundational awareness of child abuse and neglect (CAN) before they enter professional practice. Methods Using a causal-comparative design, this study assessed final-year midwifery ( n = 246) and pre-school education ( n = 115) undergraduates in Türkiye. Two validated psychometric instruments measured awareness across distinct subtypes of abuse and neglect, revealing the multifaceted nature of their understanding. Results Findings revealed a significant disparity, with future midwives being less prepared to identify CAN than their education counterparts. This awareness deficit was most pronounced for subtle forms of maltreatment, such as emotional and economic abuse, and all dimensions of neglect. A student's academic department was the sole significant predictor of awareness, outweighing the influence of academic progression or prior training. Conclusion This gap represents a systemic vulnerability cultivated by siloed higher education paradigms. Midwifery's traditional biomedical curriculum appears insufficient for imparting the holistic, socio-ecological perspective required for effective safeguarding. A paradigm shift toward mandatory Interprofessional Education (IPE) is imperative. Such reform is crucial for forging a shared professional ethos and a common language of risk, thereby creating a truly resilient and sustainable child protection framework.

custody_records.raw_content: Accompanying the enhancement of unattended systems based on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) and UAV base station, the lightweight model deployment of unattended systems is of great significance for inspecting the condition of transmission power lines and ensuring the safe and stable operation of the power grid. Current insulator defect detection methods are tasked with small–object detection in complex environments, with their accuracy often improved by optimizing network structures only. Considering both parameter and computational efficiency, we developed LFL–YOLO (LSDHead–FINs–LAMP–YOLOv8n) that is suitable for edge computing. Before the spatial pyramid transmits feature maps to the detection head, some levels are skipped based on inter–level sparsity, and the model’s ability to perceive scale and task-aware attention for complex backgrounds and small objects is dynamically enhanced. By combining this with spatial attention, a high–performance LSDHead is proposed. Secondly, a lightweight FINs is proposed to improve the neck of YOLOv8. This structure ensures effective interaction and feature penetration across different channels of local features. Finally, layer–adaptive unstructured pruning based on magnitude is performed. The pruned model not only reduces computational complexity and model size, significantly improving the model’s real–time performance, but also enhances detection accuracy. Lastly, to align more closely with real–world engineering applications, this study uses public datasets to verify the model’s generalization effect and validates the practical application effect on a dataset. Experimental results show that compared to the current benchmark, LFL–YOLO achieves significant improvements in accuracy and inference speed. Specifically, LFL–YOLO achieves an accuracy of 97.4%, compared to YOLOv8n, reduces the number of parameters by 23.5% and decreases computation by 9.6%. The proposed method has practical applicability in obtaining aerial images of transmission lines in complex environments.
